The Desert pupfish Cyprinodon macularius is a small-bodied cyprinodontid endemic to the thermal springs and saline lagoons of the Salton Sink in southern California and northern Mexico. Field surveys consistently indicate that individuals achieve an ultimate standard length of 6.08 centimeters [Li = 6.08 centimeters], a modest size reflecting the species' adaptation to highly variable and often extreme aquatic environments. Hatchlings emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably early developmental stage, with an age at birth of approximately ten days [ab = approximately ten days] when incubated at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva possesses a wet weight at birth of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter documented for other pupfish species. This initial mass imposes a tight energetic constraint on the endotrophic larva, which must rapidly develop functional feeding structures to shift to exogenous nutrition before yolk reserves are fully consumed.

A defining feature of the early life history of Desert pupfish concerns its capacity for somatic growth during the larval and juvenile stages. Under warm thermal regimes typical of their native habitats, newly emerged larvae exhibit a substantial change in length at birth of 0.0064 centimeters per day  at a water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. This rapid elongation allows a larva of roughly 3.6 millimeters standard length at hatching to double its body size within 8 weeks, underscoring the developmental pace required to exploit ephemeral desert waters. In contrast, the age at puberty is reached at 90 days [tp = 90 days] when fish are maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence. At this pivotal transition, the standard length at puberty is approximately 1.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 1.5 centimeters], a size that enables individuals to begin allocating resources toward reproductive structures rather than further somatic expansion.

Reproductive output in Cyprinodon macularius is characterized by a relatively high fecundity for a fish of its adult body mass. Females typically produce about 800 eggs per season [Ri = about 800 eggs per season] at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], with approximately 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per year] occurring repeatedly throughout the extended breeding period. This seasonal fecundity pattern allows the species to capitalize on favorable conditions in its unpredictable desert spring environment. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is 7.4 grams [Wwi = 7.4 grams], a mass that is consistent with the length-weight relationship derived from field-collected specimens. This modest adult body size constrains the absolute volume of the coelomic cavity, yet the species compensates through iteroparous spawning and the production of numerous small, adhesive eggs that are deposited on submerged vegetation or gravel substrates.

Longevity data for Desert pupfish indicate a maximum life span of 1095 days [am = 1095 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This three-year maximum is relatively short compared to some larger cyprinodontids, but it is ecologically appropriate for a species occupying thermally volatile habitats where senescence may be accelerated by high metabolic demands and periodic habitat desiccation. Comparative analyses among Cyprinodon species suggest that the total lifespan is closely linked to the thermal regime experienced during the post-juvenile phase, with warmer conditions correlating with reduced survivorship. The rapid attainment of sexual maturity and the high early reproductive investment exhibited by Desert pupfish reflect a life-history strategy that prioritizes early fecundity over extended somatic persistence. This bet-hedging approach appears adaptive in environments where the probability of adult survival across multiple breeding seasons is inherently low due to stochastic hydrological events.

Energetic demands during the critical early feeding period dictate the developmental trajectory of the yolk-sac larva once it commences exogenous feeding. At the standard temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the age at birth of 10 days [ab = 10 days] ensures that the larva begins active foraging while still utilizing residual yolk reserves, thereby buffering against variability in prey density. Field observations indicate that the standard length at puberty of 1.5 centimeters [Lp = 1.5 centimeters] corresponds to the point at which individuals can effectively compete for territories in the shallow vegetated margins of desert pools. The species reaches a maximum body size of 6.08 centimeters [Li = 6.08 centimeters] standard length, which, when combined with a maximum longevity of 3 years [am = 3 years], definitively places the Desert pupfish along the slow-fast continuum of teleost life-history variation at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. When these traits are viewed together, they paint a portrait of a highly resilient species that has evolved a suite of physiological and behavioral adaptations to persist in one of the most challenging freshwater environments on the North American continent.
